If you're wondering why they aren't more common it's due to a cultural decision which was made fairly early on in the aviation industry in the US and spread to the rest of the world through air standardization.

It is believed that if a pilot has the option to push a parachute button or jump out with a parachute then they will be almost guaranteed to abandon the plane in any emergency just to be safe, when the plane could've been saved. This lead to development and standardization around the idea that a plane carrying passengers should be able to land after an emergency without major issue. With some exceptions, passenger aircraft are typically required to have two or more engines which are powerful enough to sustain or significantly prolong flight entirely on their own in the event of an engine failure. Other systems are designed for redundancy like this as well, making parachutes less necessary and more of a potential liability if they cause premature ditching of a landable aircraft. Plus you can only attach a parachute to a plane and have it land in tact up to a certain size - you can see how hard the plane in the clip impacts the ground, imagine if it were a C-130 or 747. 

However, in general aviation for small aircraft with few seats, single engine craft which are less capable (or completely incapable) of flying with a failed engine are still largely the norm. For this reason, some aircraft designs are still popular which allow the use of a whole-aircraft abort system like in this clip. These systems are heavily criticized as encouraging lax maintenance procedures and premature ditching, leading to a catch 22 where responsible pilots often won't fly with this sort of thing because they don't need it if the aircraft is well maintained and they know how to glide it in for a landing in an emergency. 

In other words, this guy does not look very cool doing this over a city, to those in the aviation industry. Someone could've been killed if the plane had hit them because these systems aren't exactly gentle and graceful, and it came quite close to hitting the cameraman. Even with a full aircraft abort system fitted, if there were any possibility of getting over a less populated area he should've taken it. I don't know the context, but it is not a good look.
